This would indicate that the Whitewater arm is an important nursery area in Jocassee Reservoir. Applicant states that entrainment of fish eggs is not expected to be a factor at Bad Creek since the indigenous fish in Jocassee are nest builders or scatter eggs among vegetation on the bottom, free of current.
The effects of entrainment may be reduced by the deep (about 20 meters) location of the Bad Creek inlet-outlet structure. In addition, the proposed weir below the Bad Creek outlet could reduce entrainment of trout during the warm months by forming a barrier in the coldwater habitat that could deter fish from entering this area. The proposed weir could also reduce currents in the coldwater habitat, thereby reducing attractions of fish. This benefit would only exist during the stratified period, however, and might not be totally effective in that 1) some cold water would probably be drawn over the weir, and 2) trout could go over the weir by temporarily moving into the warmer upper water, particularly if attracted by flows and/or food sources. However, with the weir in place, currents from the outlet structure could be reduced in the deeper, cooler waters, thereby reducing the possibility of attracting trout.
Some fish would be expected to survive passage through the turbines and inhabit the upper reservoir. Fish residing in the upper reservoir would not be expected to reproduce because of large daily water fluctuations. Project operation would result in continual recruitment from Lake Jocassee during pumping and return of some fish during generation. An unknown percentage of the fish passed would be lost to turbine mortalities. On a cumulative basis mortalities incurred by fish passage could have a significant impact on the trout fishery in Lake Jocassee.
The area near the inlet-outlet structure in Lake Jocassee would be affected by turbid water during the initial period of operation. Under such conditions fish may migrate to other areas of Lake Jocassee. Later, fish may be attracted to the area for food after sediments and turbid water have been flushed from the upper reservoir. Organisms harmed or destroyed could create a food source for fish in the area. Trout could be attracted to the area of the proposed intake when they are seeking tributaries as spawning sites. Under such circumstances, these species would be subject to entrainment in the proposed conduits.
